fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: some words (not shown which) supplied by Mr R. O’Henley (see the note at the end of the word-list).]

item.description: a swivel used on a fishing line.

item.headword: eadar dà sgeul is dà chluais a’ chlobha
item.description: would be said regarding something which you wanted to keep secret and private.
to beat someone. “Thoill thu do gheadadh.”
crabbit. “Bha i cho oglaich.”
same as ‘oglaich’ (q.v.).
any form of surround, railing, etc. Also in the sense of a hedge.
a group of people.
“’S minig a chaill do cho aoise bliadhna an earraich dhuibh.” – refers to the working capacity of people despite their old age.
this would be said by guests when leaving the wedding reception.
a gamekeeper.
chattering. “Bha a’ chàbraid a’ dol a null ’s a nall.”
peeping.
the situation. “An t-omhnadh ’s an robh e.”
applied to a young child who would come in dripping wet.
chattering of teeth.
a hiding place.
some form of a barn dance. One can envisage the black dust in older buildings being stirred as the dancing took place.
a difficult task set before you. “Nach ann dhut a chaidh a’ ghusamaid a dheanamh an diugh.”
a V shaped piece of land which would be difficult to plough.
vomiting (cattle).
after peats had been made into ‘rubhain’ they were made into larger long stacks so that they would be easier to reach when they were being taken home.
earrings.
a brooch.
an undesirable person who you would not want in your company.
third time lucky.

item.headword: an ni a dh’fhalbhas chan e a dh’fhòghnas
item.description: refers to old traditions and says that despite the pleasure they gave, we need to move with the times and not to become too nostalgic.
an unclean, untidy person.
referring to something that had been well completed. “Bha an obair diongalta.”
an asylum.
under strict supervision.
“Chan eil treun ris nach cuirear.” – a proverb which states that despite your strength death will be the victor.

“Dh’ith thu bonnach a’ bhrosgail.” – would be said regarding people who did a certain amount of boot licking to obtain something. More usually applied to young children who would behave in this fashion go get their own way.
a jocular person.
cloudy, dark, overcast weather conditions. “Tha bùthdarus orra.”
knack. “Bha an t-alt aig air an obair.”
clerical collar.
a lead for a dog.
a medal.
because of. “Chaidh e ann air aruinn an fhear ud.”

item.headword: cha robh i dheth na h-aigh
item.description: she was not one of the best.
a small taste will lead to greed.
said to someone who was precious to you, e.g. your child. Originally refers to the sheep who was of immense valued due to the food and wool it provided.
a dirty looking person.
a small portion.
worried, anxious.
running about in a small area.
an expression used to scare off a cat. “Cudht a chait.”
throats. “Bha iad an ugain a chéile.” – they were at each other’s throats.
a likeness to someone else. “Tha suab aig a ghille sin ri mhàthair.”
the cause of. “Dh’fhoghain an deoch dha shlàinte.”
being ordered, bossed about. “Nach ann ormsa a tha a gheidhlaid.”
untidy.
protruding stomach, pot belly.
a report or rumour maybe. “Chuala mi fathann air an sin an diugh.”
a fork used for eating.
jibberish, nonsensical talk.
sneaking up on a sheep, trying to catch hold of it unawares.
* Some of above words supplied by Mr R. O’Henley.
